newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai govt likely to face big loss on rubber plan.
newsitem.headline: Thai govt likely to face big loss on rubber plan.

text.p: The Thai government is likely to suffer big losses with its current rubber price intervention plan which was aimed at shoring up sagging rubber prices, traders and industry sources said on Tuesday.
The loss is likely given declining world prices and limited warehouse space, they said.
The scheme, which was introduced in March, also affects exporters who were forced to buy expensive local products to cover contracts amid bearish world prices.
"The government is trying to please the local industry beyond its means. It will almost certainly have to shoulder a hefty loss because of this policy," said a Hat Yai-based trader.
"It is creating a two-tier system. With the world prices bearish like this, who will buy at the level it bought from local markets?" he asked.
Traders said it would be difficult to estimate how much the loss would be as that would depend on the magnitude of the government intervention and the world price movement.
In a move to help boost local rubber prices, the government is using a two-pronged policy to help lift prices in both local and export markets.
For the local market, the government has increased the minimum guaranteed prices at which it will buy unsmoked sheet rubber twice this year.
The latest hike was on May 2 when the government raised its intervention price for unsmoked grade-3 sheet rubber to 29 baht ($1.15) a kg from 27.5 baht previously.
That compared with the export price of RSS3 which was quoted at $1.09 a kg for July delivery in the FOB market.
Although exporters rarely buy rubber at the government's guaranteed prices, the intervention normally drives local prices higher.
The latest move came after thousands of rubber tappers in major rubber-producing provinces in the south held a protest last week to pressure the government to raise the prices.

The government also bought rubber in the FOB market to shore up prices as sluggish external demand caused by high stocks in major buying countries such as the United States and Japan pressured prices.
The Bank of Thailand says the value of rubber exports during the two months of this year had dropped by 16 percent.
Sanit Samosorn, deputy director general of Department of Agriculture, told Reuters the government bought more than 45,000 tonnes of RSS3 grade since March 5 and planned to buy more.
He said the government will keep the rubber and sell it when prices improve, adding that the authorities are now negotiating aggressively with potential buyers to increase sales.
But traders and industry sources said they do not expect world rubber prices to rise substantially anytime soon.
"With the winter season coming to an end, more supplies will hit the market and the prices are likely to be under downward pressure," said the Bangkok trader.
"The question is how long and how much the government can buy to prop up prices and how long it can keep the stock with limited warehouse space," he added.
Sanit said the government ran out of warehouse space for rubber stock but is negotiating to rent additional space from private sector and state enterprises.
